To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
seizures of SW and SW/PSW types are initiated in the neocortex, and that the TC neurons are disinhibited after the cortical seizures have ceased.
the neocortex is a minimal substrate for SW seizures, whereas the thalamus is a necessary substrate of seizures with SW/PSW components and of the Lennox-Gastaut type.
the minimal substrate of SW and Lennox-Gastau seizures consists of neocortical neurons, and that the majority of thalamo-cortical neurons are steadily hyper-polarized throughout these seizures.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of sleep oscillations and seizures in corticothalamocortical systems.
the neuronal substrates underlying sleep oscillations and seizures.
the neuronal substrates underlying SW seizures and of the Lenno-Gastaut type.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the thalamus is not the seat of absence seizures but rather that the thalamocortico-thalamic loop is involved.

the neuronal substrates and mechanisms underlying SW seizures are different in the two types of epilepsy, absence and Lennox-Gastuat, although both types are initiated in neopallium and propagate to the thalamocorticothalamic system.
the thalamus is not a mandatory substrate for the generation of SW seizures, but it is a mandatory substrate for SW seizures that evolve from spindles.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
sleep oscillations are a necessary substrate of absence seizures.

sleep oscillations are the most likely substrate of seizures consisting of SW complexes and SW/PSW seizures of the Lennox Gastaut type, and that the thalamus is involved as a relay station for the propagation of seizures from cortex to cortex.
SW seizures are initiated by cortical networks in which the TC system plays a permissive role.
The main takeaway from our work is that
seizures in the absence epilepsy and in the Lennox Gastaut syndrome are not initiated in the thalamus but in the neocortex.
the thalamocorticothalamic system is a substrate for sleep oscillations, which may develop into epileptic seizures.
the thalamus is not the seat of the SW seizures, as has been proposed in the past.
